before.title: 1.2 PureTech Wet Timing Belt Degradation and Oil Starvation
before.description: The 1.2 PureTech (EB2) three-cylinder petrol engine fitted to the 308 II and early 308 III uses a 'wet' timing belt that runs immersed in engine oil. The belt rubber degrades prematurely — accelerated by aged or incorrect-spec oil and fuel dilution — shedding particles that clog the oil pump pickup and the brake vacuum pump line, causing oil starvation, loss of brake servo assistance, and in the worst cases sudden catastrophic engine failure. Peugeot issued safety recalls for affected build years and Stellantis later offered a UK compensation portal plus an extended warranty of up to 10 years/112,000 miles on these engines.
before.solution: Have the belt inspected (oil filler cap check for swelling/debris) and replaced well before the original interval — UK specialists advise around 6 years/60,000 miles. If sludge is present, the oil pickup, vacuum pump line and VVT screens must be cleaned; check recall status by VIN and claim under the Stellantis extended warranty/compensation scheme where eligible. From 2023 Stellantis switched the EB2 to a chain-driven design.
symptoms: Rough running or misfires with engine management light
Hard brake pedal / reduced brake assistance
Rubber debris visible under the oil filler cap
Rattling or whining from the belt area

before.title: 1.6 HDi (DV6) Turbocharger Failure from Oil Starvation and Sludge
before.description: The 1.6 HDi diesel in the 308 I is notorious for turbocharger failure caused by oil starvation: carbon sludge — aggravated by extended oil intervals, wrong oil spec and leaking injector seals — blocks the tiny gauze filter in the turbo oil-feed banjo bolt and the feed/return pipes, starving the turbo bearing. Documented cases show oil pressure at the turbo far below the 2.3 bar minimum, and a replacement turbo fails again quickly if the sludged feed pipes, sump and pickup are not cleaned at the same time.
before.solution: Replace the turbocharger together with new oil feed and return pipes and the banjo-bolt filter, drop and clean the sump and oil pickup, and flush the engine — about $1,200-2,600 all-in at an independent shop. Prevent recurrence with strictly shortened oil-change intervals using the correct low-SAPS oil and prompt attention to injector seal leaks.
symptoms: Whining or whistling noise from the turbo
Noticeable loss of power / limp mode
Engine management light with underboost fault

before.title: 1.6 THP Intake Valve Carbon Buildup (Direct Injection)
before.description: Because the turbocharged 1.6 THP (EP6DT/EP6CDT/EP6DTS) injects fuel directly into the cylinder, no fuel washes over the backs of the intake valves; oil vapour from the PCV system bakes onto the valves and ports as hard carbon. Deposits typically become symptomatic between 50,000 and 80,000 km, progressively restricting airflow and causing rough cold idle, cold-start misfires, poor throttle response and higher fuel consumption.
before.solution: Walnut-shell blasting of the intake ports and valves is the accepted fix (roughly $350-900 at independent specialists; dealer quotes can be far higher) and is worth repeating preventively every 50,000-60,000 km. Quality fuel and regular oil changes slow, but do not prevent, re-accumulation.

before.title: 1.6 THP/VTi (EP6 'Prince') Timing Chain Stretch and Cold-Start Rattle
before.description: The PSA/BMW co-developed 1.6 'Prince' engine (EP6 VTi and EP6DT/EP6CDT THP) in the 308 I and early 308 II suffers well-documented timing chain stretch, often before 100,000 km. The original chain was too narrow for the load and the hydraulic tensioner bleeds down overnight, producing the characteristic 'death rattle' on cold start; left unaddressed the chain can skip teeth, throwing valve timing out and risking severe valve/piston damage. PSA revised the chain, tensioner and guides (brown-to-white PVC guides) around 2012-2013, and extended oil-change intervals are a known aggravating factor.
before.solution: Replace the timing chain kit (chain, tensioner, guides, sprockets) with the latest revised parts as soon as rattle or cam/crank correlation faults appear — roughly $800-2,000 at an independent specialist. Shorten oil change intervals to about 6,000 miles/10,000 km with the correct low-SAPS 5W-30 to slow wear.
symptoms: Metallic rattle for a few seconds on cold start
Constant chain rattle at idle once stretch worsens
Engine management light with cam/crank correlation faults
Loss of power or limp mode

before.title: EAT6 Automatic Gearbox Shudder and Jerky Low-Speed Shifting
before.description: The Aisin-built EAT6 six-speed automatic fitted to the 308 II has a widespread reputation for low-speed shudder and jerky shifts, particularly when cold, in crawling traffic, and immediately after stop/start restarts. Causes documented by UK gearbox specialists include degraded transmission fluid affecting torque converter lock-up, valve body spool deposits, worn clutch packs and outdated TCU software; ignored shudder accelerates torque converter and clutch wear.
before.solution: First steps are a transmission fluid and filter change with the correct Aisin specification fluid plus a dealer TCU software update, which resolves many cases for a few hundred dollars. Persistent shudder points to the torque converter or valve body, which cost roughly $1,500-3,500 to repair or replace at an independent gearbox specialist.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration pulling away at low speed
Jerky or harsh gearshifts when cold
Lurch or judder after a stop/start restart
Delayed engagement selecting Drive or Reverse
Gearbox warning light in advanced cases

before.title: Electric Parking Brake (EPB) Faults — Caliper Motor, Switch and Wiring
before.description: 308 II (T9) and later cars with the electric parking brake commonly throw a 'Parking brake fault' message with a flashing warning lamp, the brake refusing to release or failing to auto-apply. Documented root causes across owner forums include failure of the electric actuator motors on the rear calipers (water ingress/electrical failure), a worn EPB console switch, wiring harness faults, and a weak 12V battery; faults also frequently appear after rear pad changes if the actuators are not wound back and recalibrated with a diagnostic tool.
before.solution: Diagnose with a Peugeot-compatible scan tool first: a worn switch or weak battery is a cheap fix, while a failed caliper actuator motor requires a replacement motor or caliper followed by EPB recalibration. After any rear brake work, the actuators must be retracted and recalibrated electronically to avoid inducing the fault.
symptoms: 'Parking brake fault' message on instrument panel
Handbrake will not release or car feels held back
Parking brake fails to apply automatically
Fault appears intermittently or after rear pad replacement
